title: SwiftUI Fundamentals & Layout
scopeHtml: Scope: Declarative UI, views, modifiers and their order, stacks, frames, layout system, Compose comparison.

notes.title: Baseline and the mental model
notes.html:
Baseline for this whole track. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 as the minimum deployment target, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials. We use @Observable, NavigationStack, SwiftData, async/await, actors and Swift Testing. Legacy forms (ObservableObject, NavigationView, Core Data, Combine, XCTest) appear only under "you will meet this in old codebases". Anything new in iOS 18/26 is marked verify.

Android equivalent first. In Android you describe UI with Jetpack Compose: @Composable functions that re-run when state they read changes (recomposition). In iOS the same idea is SwiftUI: UI is a function of state, written declaratively. The big difference is the shape of the building block. A composable is a function. A SwiftUI view is a struct (a value type) that conforms to the View protocol and exposes a body property.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import SwiftUI

struct Greeting: View {
    let name: String

    var body: some View {
        Text("Hello, \(name)")
            .font(.title)
    }
}
@Composable
fun Greeting(name: String) {
    Text(
        text = "Hello, $name",
        style = MaterialTheme.typography.headlineMedium
    )
}

The mental model. Both frameworks follow: UI = f(state). You never say "set the label's text"; you say "when the name is X, this is what the screen looks like" and the framework diffs and updates.

Android (Compose) iOS (SwiftUI)
@Composable fun struct X: View with var body
Modifier chain passed as parameter Modifier methods chained on the view
remember { mutableStateOf() } @State
Column / Row / Box VStack / HStack / ZStack
Spacer(Modifier.weight(1f)) Spacer()
@Preview #Preview
LazyColumn List / LazyVStack
Arrangement / Alignment spacing: / alignment: parameters
Recomposition with skipping Re-evaluation of body with diffing

Where it differs in practice.

  • In Compose, the function is the unit of recomposition, and the compiler plugin injects a hidden Composer parameter and a slot table. In SwiftUI, there is no compiler plugin and no slot table you can see. SwiftUI keeps an attribute graph (a dependency graph) separate from your structs. Your View structs are thrown away and recreated constantly; they are cheap descriptions, not the live objects.
  • Compose modifiers are a parameter (modifier: Modifier) that you thread through. SwiftUI modifiers are methods that each wrap the view in a new view type.
  • SwiftUI is stricter about layout: a parent proposes a size, a child chooses its own size, the parent positions it. Compose uses constraints (min/max) that are passed down.

Real industry examples. Apple's own apps (Weather, Stocks widgets, Settings in iOS 17+) are SwiftUI. Airbnb and Lyft have publicly talked about adopting SwiftUI feature by feature inside UIKit apps, using UIHostingController to embed it. The Point-Free team's Swift Composable Architecture is built on SwiftUI's value-type idea.

Everyday analogy. A SwiftUI view struct is like a printed restaurant order slip. The kitchen (SwiftUI runtime) keeps the real dishes in progress. You can print a fresh slip every second at almost zero cost; the kitchen compares the new slip with the old one and only changes the dishes that differ.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "a SwiftUI View is a UI object like UIView". It is not; it is a lightweight value description, and the heavy rendered objects are owned by SwiftUI.
  • Saying "body is called only once". It is re-evaluated whenever a dependency changes, and the struct itself is re-created by the parent.
  • Android vs iOS: in Compose you can put side effects loosely in a composable and guard them with LaunchedEffect; in SwiftUI the equivalent is .task, and body must stay free of side effects.

notes.title: The View protocol and body
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose a screen is any function annotated @Composable. In SwiftUI you conform a struct to View, which has exactly one requirement: var body: some View.

public protocol View {
    associatedtype Body: View
    @ViewBuilder @MainActor var body: Self.Body { get }
}

In Swift 6 / iOS 18 SDKs View is @MainActor-isolated (verify exact isolation of body in the SDK you build with). This is why view code can touch main-actor state without extra annotation, and why you get errors when you call main-actor view code from a background context.

What some View means. some View is an opaque return type: "a single concrete type that conforms to View, which the compiler knows but I do not spell out". Text("a").padding().background(.red) has a type like ModifiedContent<ModifiedContent<Text, _PaddingLayout>, _BackgroundStyleModifier<Color>>. You never want to write that, so some View hides it. The type is still static, so SwiftUI can diff trees without reflection at runtime for most of the work.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct ProfileHeader: View {
    let user: User

    var body: some View {
        HStack {
            AsyncImage(url: user.avatarURL)
                .frame(width: 48, height: 48)
                .clipShape(Circle())
            VStack(alignment: .leading) {
                Text(user.name).font(.headline)
                Text(user.handle).font(.subheadline).foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            }
        }
    }
}
@Composable
fun ProfileHeader(user: User) {
    Row {
        AsyncImage(
            model = user.avatarUrl,
            contentDescription = null,
            modifier = Modifier.size(48.dp).clip(CircleShape)
        )
        Column {
            Text(user.name, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium)
            Text(user.handle, color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onSurfaceVariant)
        }
    }
}

Rules for body.

  • It must be a pure description. No network calls, no timers, no mutating state, no heavy sorting. SwiftUI can call it many times, at any time, on the main thread.
  • It should be fast: a slow body shows up as hitches in Instruments' SwiftUI template (View Body track) and as dropped frames.
  • Returning different concrete types from different branches of a plain if is an error unless you use @ViewBuilder (see the ViewBuilder section).

Why value types. Structs are copied, not shared. A view cannot be mutated by someone else behind its back, and there is no inheritance tree like UIView. A struct with a few stored properties lives on the stack or inline in its parent; there is no heap allocation and no ARC traffic per view, unlike UIView objects, each of which is a heap object (and backed by a CALayer). That is the performance reason Apple chose structs.

Real industry examples. Apple's WWDC sessions "Demystify SwiftUI" and "Data Essentials in SwiftUI" explain identity and lifetime; teams at Airbnb and Lyft describe breaking big screens into many small View structs, which is cheap precisely because they are structs.

Everyday analogy. body is a recipe card, not the cooked meal. You can rewrite the card as often as you like; nobody starts cooking again unless the card changed in a way that matters.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming you can store a @State in a class-based view. Views are structs; state is held by SwiftUI outside the struct.
  • Putting print or DispatchQueue work in body. It runs repeatedly. Use Self._printChanges() only for debugging (it is underscored, undocumented, remove before shipping).
  • Mixing up "some View" and "any View". some is one fixed hidden type (fast, static); any View is an existential box (dynamic, slower, loses identity information).

notes.title: View identity and lifetime
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Compose decides which remembered state belongs to which call by position in the composition plus optional key(...). SwiftUI uses identity with two flavours: structural identity (position in the view tree) and explicit identity (.id(_:) or Identifiable in ForEach).

Structural identity. The type and position of a view in the body hierarchy identify it. An if/else creates two different structural positions:

var body: some View {
    if isLoggedIn {
        HomeView()      // identity A
    } else {
        LoginView()     // identity B
    }
}

When isLoggedIn flips, HomeView is destroyed (its @State is lost) and LoginView is created. That is the same as a Compose if branch leaving the composition, which disposes its remembered values.

Explicit identity. .id(value) forces a new identity when value changes. It is the SwiftUI equivalent of Compose's key(value) { ... } block, and it is the standard trick to reset a view's internal state:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
DetailView(item: item)
    .id(item.id)   // new item -> old DetailView state thrown away
key(item.id) {
    DetailScreen(item)
}

Lifetime vs value. A view value (the struct) is recreated on every parent body evaluation. The view's lifetime (its identity in the graph, along with its @State storage) lasts as long as it stays at the same structural position with the same identity. This distinction is the root of most "my state got reset" bugs (see the State track note, 03_S1).

Why AnyView is discouraged. Wrapping in AnyView erases the static type, so SwiftUI can no longer tell cheaply whether two branches have the same shape. This hurts diffing and animations. Prefer @ViewBuilder, Group, or a generic parameter.

Production incident pattern. A list of cards animates strangely and loses scroll/text-field state when new data arrives because ForEach(items.indices, id: \.self) is used: the index is the identity, so inserting at the top shifts every identity. Use a stable model id.

Real industry examples. Instagram-style feeds, Spotify-style playlists: everything in a feed uses stable server ids as identity so that likes and inserts animate correctly.

Everyday analogy. Identity is a seat number in a cinema. If you swap which person sits in seat 12, the seat is the same, the person changed. If the cinema renumbers all seats when one person leaves, everyone looks like they moved.

Common interview traps.

  • Using id: \.self on non-unique or mutable data, causing duplicate-id warnings or wrong animations.
  • Believing .id() is free. It destroys and recreates the subtree, losing state and re-running .task.
  • Android vs iOS: Compose recomposes by position only unless you add key; SwiftUI additionally uses type, so changing a branch type resets state even without .id.

notes.title: Modifiers and why order matters
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose, Modifier.padding(16.dp).background(Color.Red) is an ordered chain, and order changes the result (padding before background shrinks the coloured area). SwiftUI works the same way, but each modifier is a method that returns a new view that wraps the previous one.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
Text("Hi")
    .padding()
    .background(.red)      // red box includes the padding
Text(
    "Hi",
    modifier = Modifier
        .background(Color.Red)   // red now includes the padding
        .padding(16.dp)
)

Careful: the reading order is inverted. In Compose the first modifier is the outermost (it constrains everything after it), so padding().background() would colour only the content. In SwiftUI the first modifier is the innermost wrapper and later ones wrap around it, so the SwiftUI .padding().background(.red) translates to Compose Modifier.background(Red).padding(16.dp). This is a classic cross-platform mix-up.

Walkthrough.

Text("Hi").padding().background(.red)   // red area = text + padding
Text("Hi").background(.red).padding()   // red area = text only; padding is transparent outside

How it works: .padding() produces ModifiedContent<Text, _PaddingLayout>. .background(.red) then wraps that, so the background fills the padded size. In the second order, background wraps only Text, then padding wraps the red text.

Frame order.

Text("Tap")
    .frame(width: 200, height: 44)   // a 200x44 flexible container
    .background(.blue)               // blue fills 200x44
    .padding(8)                      // outer 8pt margin, not coloured

Text("Tap")
    .background(.blue)               // blue hugs the text
    .frame(width: 200, height: 44)   // frame is invisible, centred around it

Tap target gotcha. Hit-testing follows the shape of the view at that point in the chain. To make a whole padded row tappable use .contentShape(Rectangle()) before .onTapGesture/Button, because transparent areas and Spacer are not tappable by default.

Environment-style modifiers. Some modifiers (.font, .foregroundStyle, .tint, .disabled, .environment) do not wrap layout; they write into the environment, which flows to all descendants. Order matters less for them, but a child can override a parent. Other modifiers such as .padding, .frame, .background, .overlay, .clipShape, .offset are layout/drawing modifiers and order matters strongly.

Common compile-time cost. Very long modifier chains with complex generic types are one source of the "The compiler is unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time" error. Fix by extracting subviews or computed properties.

Real industry examples. Design-system libraries (Airbnb's open source work, Mercury, Lyft's) wrap repeated modifier chains in a custom ViewModifier or a view extension so that "primary button style" is one call.

Everyday analogy. Modifiers are layers of gift wrapping. Wrapping paper then a ribbon looks different from a ribbon then paper; each layer wraps what is already there.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting .background before .padding to colour the padding.
  • Putting .frame after .background and wondering why the colour did not stretch.
  • Android vs iOS: believing Compose and SwiftUI modifier order read the same way; they invert for layout intent.
  • Forgetting .contentShape and asking why a Spacer-padded row ignores taps.

notes.title: Stacks, Spacer and alignment
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Column, Row, Box become VStack, HStack, ZStack. Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp) becomes spacing: 8. Alignment.Start becomes alignment: .leading. Modifier.weight(1f) becomes Spacer() (or .frame(maxWidth: .infinity)).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
    Text("Title").font(.headline)
    Text("Subtitle").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    HStack {
        Text("Price")
        Spacer()
        Text("$9.99")
    }
}
.padding()
Column(
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp),
    horizontalAlignment = Alignment.Start,
    modifier = Modifier.padding(16.dp)
) {
    Text("Title", style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium)
    Text("Subtitle", color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onSurfaceVariant)
    Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.SpaceBetween) {
        Text("Price")
        Text("$9.99")
    }
}

How stacks size themselves.

  • A stack takes the size its children need (hugging) plus spacing, up to what its parent proposes. It does not expand to fill the screen unless a child is flexible.
  • Spacer() is a flexible view with a minimum length (system default) that expands to absorb remaining space along the stack's axis. Color, Rectangle, Divider and GeometryReader are also greedy.
  • default spacing in stacks is adaptive: nil spacing asks each pair of children for their preferred distance (e.g. text-to-text distance differs from image-to-text). Pass spacing: 0 to remove it.

ZStack and overlays. ZStack layers children, last on top, aligned by alignment: .center by default. For a decoration that should not influence layout use .overlay or .background rather than a ZStack child: the base view dictates size and the decoration follows.

Image("cover")
    .resizable().scaledToFill()
    .frame(height: 200)
    .clipped()
    .overlay(alignment: .bottomLeading) {
        Text("Featured").padding(8).background(.ultraThinMaterial)
    }

Alignment guides. Alignment in SwiftUI is based on named guides (.leading, .firstTextBaseline, .center...). You can customise with .alignmentGuide(.leading) { d in d[.trailing] } or define a custom VerticalAlignment so two sibling views in different containers align to a shared line. Compose has alignBy / AlignmentLine for the same job; baseline alignment (HStack(alignment: .firstTextBaseline)) is the common daily use.

Layout priority. When there is not enough room, layoutPriority(_:) decides who gets truncated last, similar to Compose weights/intrinsic measurement. .fixedSize() makes a view take its ideal size ignoring the parent proposal (useful for multi-line text that must not truncate).

Real industry examples. Banking and e-commerce apps (Cash App style rows, Airbnb listing cards) use HStack/Spacer rows with .firstTextBaseline alignment for price rows and lineLimit with layoutPriority for names.

Everyday analogy. A stack is a bookshelf: books stand side by side (HStack) or are piled up (VStack). Spacer is the empty gap at the end of the shelf that pushes books to the left or to both sides.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting HStack to fill the width. It hugs content; add Spacer() or .frame(maxWidth: .infinity).
  • Using a ZStack for decorations that then inflate the layout.
  • Android vs iOS: there is no weight; two equal-width children use .frame(maxWidth: .infinity) on both, or a Grid.
  • Forgetting alignment: applies to the stack's cross axis only.

notes.title: The layout system: propose, choose, place
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Android's View system measures with MeasureSpec; Compose passes Constraints (min and max width/height) down and returns a size. SwiftUI uses a three-step negotiation.

  1. The parent proposes a size to the child (a ProposedViewSize, each dimension can be a number, nil = ideal size, 0 = minimum, or .infinity).
  2. The child chooses its own size (the parent must respect it).
  3. The parent places the child inside its own coordinate space.
Parent                      Child
  | -- propose 300x600 -->    |
  |                           | Text: "I need 120x20"
  | <-- 120x20 ------------   |
  | place child at centre     |

Consequences.

  • Text picks the size of its content (truncating if the proposal is smaller). Image (non-resizable) uses its natural pixel size. .resizable() makes it accept any proposal.
  • .frame(width:height:) is not "set the child to this size". It is a wrapper view with its own fixed size that proposes the child the same size, then centres the child. If the child refuses (a non-resizable image), the frame stays and the child overflows or floats inside it.
  • .frame(maxWidth: .infinity) makes a flexible wrapper that takes the max of what the parent proposes. This is the most common "fill width" idiom.
  • .padding shrinks the proposal by the padding, asks the child, then adds the padding back to the answer.
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
Image("photo")
    .resizable()
    .scaledToFit()
    .frame(maxWidth: .infinity)
Image(
    painter = painterResource(R.drawable.photo),
    contentDescription = null,
    contentScale = ContentScale.Fit,
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth()
)

Safe areas. SwiftUI automatically insets content away from the notch, Dynamic Island, home indicator and keyboard. Backgrounds that should bleed use .ignoresSafeArea(). Android's edge-to-edge (enforced from Android 15) with WindowInsets is the analogue, but SwiftUI does it by default, which many Android devs find easier.

Dynamic Type. Fonts scale with the user's text-size setting. Layouts must tolerate large sizes; test at "Accessibility XXL". @ScaledMetric scales custom numbers (icon sizes) with Dynamic Type.

Real industry examples. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines expect Dynamic Type support; apps rejected in accessibility audits or flagged by enterprise customers often break at accessibility sizes (clipped text in HStack rows).

Everyday analogy. The parent is a landlord offering a flat of up to a certain size; the tenant (child) decides how much of it they actually use; the landlord then decides where in the building the tenant's space goes.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing .frame as "resizing the child". It wraps and proposes.
  • Using hard-coded sizes everywhere, which breaks on iPad, landscape and Dynamic Type.
  • Android vs iOS: a child cannot demand more than its parent allows in Compose (constraints); in SwiftUI a child can legally return a size bigger than proposed, and the parent just positions it (overflow).
  • Forgetting .ignoresSafeArea applies per edge/region and to backgrounds, not content that must stay readable.

notes.title: GeometryReader, containers and anchor tools
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. BoxWithConstraints or onSizeChanged + Layout in Compose. In SwiftUI the tool is GeometryReader, which gives you a GeometryProxy with size, safeAreaInsets and frame(in:).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct HalfWidthBar: View {
    var body: some View {
        GeometryReader { proxy in
            Rectangle()
                .fill(.blue)
                .frame(width: proxy.size.width * 0.5, height: 8)
        }
        .frame(height: 8)
    }
}
@Composable
fun HalfWidthBar() {
    BoxWithConstraints(Modifier.height(8.dp)) {
        Box(
            Modifier
                .width(maxWidth * 0.5f)
                .height(8.dp)
                .background(Color.Blue)
        )
    }
}

Gotchas.

  • GeometryReader is greedy: it takes all proposed space, like a Color. Unconstrained inside a VStack it eats the remaining height. Always bound it with .frame or put it in .background/.overlay of a view whose size you want to measure.
  • Children inside are positioned at the top-left, not centred.
  • It can cause extra layout passes. Overuse is a performance smell.

Modern alternatives (iOS 16-18, verify exact availability).

  • .onGeometryChange(for:of:action:) (back-deployed to iOS 16 in the iOS 18 SDK; verify) reads size without embedding a GeometryReader.
  • containerRelativeFrame(_:) (iOS 17) sizes a view as a fraction of its container, e.g. carousel cards: .containerRelativeFrame(.horizontal, count: 3, spacing: 8).
  • ScrollView with .scrollTargetBehavior(.viewAligned) and .scrollPosition (iOS 17) replaces many hacks that used GeometryReader and preference keys.
  • PreferenceKey passes values up the tree (child to ancestor); the classic way to measure a child's size and use it elsewhere.
struct SizeKey: PreferenceKey {
    static let defaultValue: CGSize = .zero
    static func reduce(value: inout CGSize, nextValue: () -> CGSize) { value = nextValue() }
}

extension View {
    func readSize(_ onChange: @escaping (CGSize) -> Void) -> some View {
        background(GeometryReader { Color.clear.preference(key: SizeKey.self, value: $0.size) })
            .onPreferenceChange(SizeKey.self, perform: onChange)
    }
}

In Swift 6 mode, a static var defaultValue that is mutable triggers a concurrency error; use static let as shown (this is a very common migration warning).

Real industry examples. Parallax headers (Spotify album screen), custom sliders and carousels read geometry. Apple's Photos-style zoom transitions use matched geometry (see the animations note 02_U2).

Everyday analogy. GeometryReader is a tape measure that also happens to be a very large piece of furniture: handy for measuring, but placed carelessly it takes up the whole room.

Common interview traps.

  • Wrapping whole screens in GeometryReader "just in case".
  • Reading proxy.size and storing it in @State without guarding against layout feedback loops.
  • Mutable static var defaultValue in PreferenceKey under Swift 6.
  • Android vs iOS: BoxWithConstraints gives constraints (max), GeometryReader gives the proposed size, which is not always the final size.

notes.title: Layout protocol, ViewThatFits, Grid and adaptive UI
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose you write a custom Layout { measurables, constraints -> ... }, use FlowRow, LazyVerticalGrid and WindowSizeClass for adaptive screens. SwiftUI has the Layout protocol, ViewThatFits, Grid and size classes.

The Layout protocol (iOS 16+). You implement two methods: sizeThatFits (given a proposal, return your size) and placeSubviews (position children). It is the SwiftUI equivalent of Compose's Layout.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct EqualWidthHStack: Layout {
    func sizeThatFits(proposal: ProposedViewSize, subviews: Subviews, cache: inout ()) -> CGSize {
        let widest = subviews.map { $0.sizeThatFits(.unspecified).width }.max() ?? 0
        let height = subviews.map { $0.sizeThatFits(.unspecified).height }.max() ?? 0
        return CGSize(width: widest * CGFloat(subviews.count), height: height)
    }

    func placeSubviews(in bounds: CGRect, proposal: ProposedViewSize, subviews: Subviews, cache: inout ()) {
        let w = bounds.width / CGFloat(max(subviews.count, 1))
        for (i, sub) in subviews.enumerated() {
            sub.place(
                at: CGPoint(x: bounds.minX + w * CGFloat(i), y: bounds.minY),
                proposal: ProposedViewSize(width: w, height: bounds.height)
            )
        }
    }
}
@Composable
fun EqualWidthRow(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    Layout(content) { measurables, constraints ->
        val w = constraints.maxWidth / maxOf(measurables.size, 1)
        val placeables = measurables.map { it.measure(Constraints.fixedWidth(w)) }
        val h = placeables.maxOfOrNull { it.height } ?: 0
        layout(constraints.maxWidth, h) {
            placeables.forEachIndexed { i, p -> p.placeRelative(i * w, 0) }
        }
    }
}

Usage: EqualWidthHStack { Text("A"); Text("Long label"); Text("C") }. Layout instances are cached by the system; the cache parameter avoids repeated measuring.

ViewThatFits (iOS 16+). Gives it several alternatives and shows the first one that fits the proposed space. Ideal for "horizontal on iPad, vertical on iPhone / when text is large".

ViewThatFits {
    HStack { icon; title; Spacer(); actionButton }   // try wide first
    VStack(alignment: .leading) { HStack { icon; title }; actionButton }  // fall back
}

Grid (iOS 16+) vs LazyVGrid.

  • Grid + GridRow lays out a small, fully rendered table with column alignment (labels and values), like a Compose Row of Columns or a table. Not lazy.
  • LazyVGrid with GridItem(.adaptive(minimum: 120)) builds large scrolling grids lazily (see 02_U2).
Grid(alignment: .leading, horizontalSpacing: 12, verticalSpacing: 8) {
    GridRow { Text("Name"); Text(user.name) }
    GridRow { Text("Plan"); Text(user.plan) }
}

Adaptive layout tools.

  • @Environment(\.horizontalSizeClass) is .compact or .regular. iPhone portrait is compact; iPad full screen is regular; iPad split view and Stage Manager can make an iPad compact, so never test for device idiom to decide layout.
  • NavigationSplitView provides sidebar/content/detail and collapses automatically on iPhone (see the navigation note).
  • ContainerRelativeShape, containerRelativeFrame and ViewThatFits handle widgets and cards.
  • Compose parallels: WindowSizeClass, NavigationSuiteScaffold, ListDetailPaneScaffold.

Real industry examples. The Mail and Notes apps use split views; Slack on iPad uses a regular size class for a sidebar; Airbnb adapts card grids with adaptive columns.

Everyday analogy. ViewThatFits is trying outfits: you try the fancy one, and if it does not fit, you put on the next.

Common interview traps.

  • Branching on UIDevice.current.userInterfaceIdiom instead of size class; breaks in multitasking.
  • Using Grid for thousands of rows (non-lazy, builds everything).
  • Forgetting the cache generic parameter and measuring subviews multiple times in a custom Layout.
  • Android vs iOS: LazyVerticalGrid(GridCells.Adaptive) equals LazyVGrid with .adaptive; Compose Grid has no direct equivalent to SwiftUI Grid.

notes.title: ViewBuilder and conditional views
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose, a @Composable () -> Unit lambda can contain statements, if, for, when. In SwiftUI a closure that returns content is annotated with @ViewBuilder, a result builder that turns a list of view expressions into a single tuple view.

VStack {
    Text("A")
    Text("B")
    if showBadge { Badge() }
    ForEach(items) { Row(item: $0) }
}

The compiler rewrites this to roughly VStack { TupleView(Text, Text, Optional<Badge>, ForEach<...>) }. Older SDKs supported at most 10 direct children per builder (buildBlock overloads up to 10); wrap in Group or ForEach if you hit "extra argument in call". Newer SDKs use parameter packs (TupleView with variadic generics, verify the current limit in your Xcode).

Conditionals.

  • if / else and switch are supported by ViewBuilder. Each branch is a different structural identity (see identity section), and SwiftUI animates between them as insertion/removal.
  • if let works: if let user { ProfileView(user: user) }.
  • Prefer modifiers with parameters over conditionals when you only change an attribute: .opacity(isOn ? 1 : 0.4) keeps identity, so state and animations survive.
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@ViewBuilder
private var content: some View {
    switch viewModel.state {
    case .loading: ProgressView()
    case .loaded(let items): ItemList(items: items)
    case .failed(let error): ErrorView(message: error.localizedDescription)
    }
}
@Composable
private fun Content(state: UiState) {
    when (state) {
        UiState.Loading -> CircularProgressIndicator()
        is UiState.Loaded -> ItemList(state.items)
        is UiState.Failed -> ErrorView(state.error.message.orEmpty())
    }
}

Custom container views. Pass content with @ViewBuilder let content: () -> Content and a generic Content: View; this is how Card { ... } wrappers are written (like a slot API content: @Composable () -> Unit).

struct Card<Content: View>: View {
    @ViewBuilder let content: () -> Content

    var body: some View {
        content()
            .padding()
            .background(.background, in: RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12))
            .shadow(radius: 2)
    }
}

What is not allowed. Arbitrary statements like let x = ...; print(x) inside a builder closure are limited: let declarations are fine in newer Swift, but expressions returning Void (like print) cause errors. Move logic into computed properties or functions.

Real industry examples. Design systems expose slot-style APIs: Section { rows } header: { Text("...") } in Form and List themselves follow this pattern; the TCA library builds Reducer result builders in the same style.

Everyday analogy. A @ViewBuilder is a tray: you set several plates on it and it hands the waiter one tray.

Common interview traps.

  • Using if to toggle a modifier and unknowingly resetting @State.
  • Hitting the "10 views" limit on older Xcode; use Group.
  • Returning different view types from a computed property without @ViewBuilder or Group (error: "function declares an opaque return type, but the return statements in its body do not have matching underlying types").
  • Android vs iOS: Compose conditionals dispose state similarly, but modifiers in Compose can be conditionally applied via then, which does not change identity.

notes.title: Previews with #Preview
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. @Preview on a composable in Android Studio, with parameters like showBackground, uiMode, @PreviewParameter. In Xcode 15+ you use the #Preview macro next to the view.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
#Preview("Dark, large text") {
    ProfileHeader(user: .sample)
        .preferredColorScheme(.dark)
        .environment(\.dynamicTypeSize, .accessibility3)
}
@Preview(name = "Dark, large text", uiMode = UI_MODE_NIGHT_YES, fontScale = 2f)
@Composable
fun ProfileHeaderPreview() {
    ProfileHeader(user = sampleUser)
}

Practical rules.

  • Give previews sample data (static let sample) and avoid network calls; previews run in a separate process (XCPreviewAgent), and failures there are the most common "Preview crashed" cause.
  • For stateful views, use @Previewable @State var x = 0 (Swift 6 / Xcode 16, verify) so you can pass $x to a child. The legacy workaround is a small wrapper struct holding @State.
  • SwiftData previews use an in-memory ModelContainer passed via .modelContainer(for:inMemory:).
  • Preview traits: #Preview(traits: .landscapeLeft) or .sizeThatFitsLayout (verify exact names in your SDK).
  • Multiple #Preview blocks in one file show a variant gallery: light, dark, Dynamic Type, right-to-left (.environment(\.layoutDirection, .rightToLeft)), and localisation (.environment(\.locale, ...)).

Legacy form you will meet.

struct ProfileHeader_Previews: PreviewProvider {
    static var previews: some View { ProfileHeader(user: .sample) }
}

Common preview errors and fixes.

  • "Cannot preview in this file / Failed to build": the whole target must compile; one error in any file blocks all previews. Fix the build first.
  • Missing environment object or @Environment value crashes the preview at launch: inject it in the preview.
  • Previews of views that need @MainActor singletons: create sample dependencies, never use production singletons.
  • Slow previews: a huge module or a heavy asset catalog; split features into Swift packages so previews build a smaller module.
  • Canvas shows stale output: "Restart preview" or clean the build folder; Editor > Canvas > Diagnostics helps (verify menu names).

Real industry examples. Teams at large apps (Airbnb, Lyft) keep feature code in local Swift packages with sample-data "preview apps" so the preview builds in seconds. Point-Free's isowords and TCA examples also lean on previews with stubbed dependencies.

Everyday analogy. A preview is a fitting room: you try the view in many conditions before it goes on the shop floor.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling real APIs, Keychain or Firebase in previews, causing crashes.
  • Forgetting the legacy PreviewProvider still exists in older codebases.
  • Android vs iOS: @Preview is interactive on Android only in "Interactive mode"; SwiftUI previews are live by default in Xcode (taps work in Live mode).

notes.title: SwiftUI versus Compose in practice
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. This section is a comparison cheat sheet to answer the classic interview question "you know Compose, how would you compare it with SwiftUI?".

Concern Compose SwiftUI
Unit of UI @Composable function View struct
Update trigger State read in composition Property wrapper / @Observable dependency
Granularity Recomposition scope (lambda) Whole body of the dependent view
Skipping Stability inference, @Stable Struct equality + dependency tracking (Equatable helps)
Side effects LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect .task, .onAppear, .onChange, .onDisappear
Remembered state remember, rememberSaveable @State, @SceneStorage
Modifier order Left to right outside-in Inside-out wrapping
Lists LazyColumn List, LazyVStack
Theming MaterialTheme Environment + system styles
Preview @Preview #Preview
Interop AndroidView / ComposeView UIViewRepresentable / UIHostingController
Build tool Gradle + Compose compiler plugin Xcode, SwiftPM, no extra plugin

Where SwiftUI is easier. System look and feel come for free: navigation bars, lists with swipe actions, forms, dynamic type, dark mode and accessibility are mostly automatic. Animations are a one-liner (withAnimation).

Where SwiftUI is harder. Fine-grained layout control is trickier than Compose's constraints; behaviours changed between iOS versions (for example ScrollView and List internals changed in iOS 17/18), so some bugs exist only on specific OS versions. You must test on the minimum deployment target. Undocumented behaviours of List, NavigationStack and keyboard handling appear in production regularly.

When SwiftUI is not enough (UIKit interop). Rich text editing, complex collection layouts, advanced camera, maps customisation, UIPageViewController behaviours. Host UIKit with UIViewRepresentable/UIViewControllerRepresentable, or host SwiftUI in UIKit with UIHostingController. See the UIKit notes in this track.

Real industry examples. Many large apps use SwiftUI for new screens and keep UIKit for the existing core. The migration pattern is exactly what Android teams do moving from Views to Compose with ComposeView.

Everyday analogy. Compose and SwiftUI are two brands of the same type of kitchen appliance: the buttons are in different places and the ordering of the steps is inverted, but you cook the same dishes.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming SwiftUI recomposition equals Compose recomposition scoping. SwiftUI re-evaluates the dependent view's whole body; there is no lambda-level scope.
  • Saying SwiftUI "has no performance problems because it is declarative". Heavy body work, unstable identity and large non-lazy stacks all hurt.
  • Android vs iOS: assuming SwiftUI features ship independently of the OS; they are tied to the iOS version, so minimum target limits API availability (@available).

notes.title: Common errors and what they mean
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Compose gives errors like "Modifier chain order surprises" or "Reading a state in the wrong scope". SwiftUI errors are mostly compiler errors about opaque types and builders, plus a handful of runtime warnings.

Message Meaning and fix
"Type 'any View' cannot conform to 'View'" Used any View where some View is needed; use AnyView, generics or @ViewBuilder.
"Function declares an opaque return type, but the return statements do not have matching underlying types" Different concrete types in branches; add @ViewBuilder or Group.
"The compiler is unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time" Expression too complex; split subviews, add explicit types.
"Extra argument in call" (more than 10 children, older SDK) Wrap children in Group.
"Modifying state during view update, this will cause undefined behavior" (runtime) You mutated @State or observable data inside body. Move it to .onAppear, .task or an action.
"Publishing changes from within view updates is not allowed" (legacy ObservableObject) Same cause; dispatch after the update or fix the data flow.
"Accessing State's value outside of being installed on a View" Reading a @State of a view not yet in the hierarchy (for example in init).
Duplicate ids in ForEach Non-unique id; use a unique stable id.
"Cannot find 'X' in scope" for @Observable Missing import Observation (usually implied by import SwiftUI), or wrong target.
Preview crashes at launch Missing environment or heavy dependency; inject sample objects.

Concurrency errors in Swift 6 mode. Calling a @MainActor-isolated view model from a nonisolated context, capturing non-Sendable values in Task { }, or mutable static var in PreferenceKey/EnvironmentKey produce hard errors in Swift 6 mode and warnings in Swift 5 mode with strict concurrency. Mark view models @MainActor @Observable.

Layout debugging tools.

  • .border(.red) or .background(.red.opacity(0.2)) on suspects to see real frames.
  • Xcode View Debugger (Debug > View Debugging) and the SwiftUI Instruments template (View Body, View Properties, Core Animation commits) to see which views re-evaluate and why.
  • Self._printChanges() inside body (debug only, undocumented).
  • Accessibility Inspector for label and Dynamic Type checks.

Production incident patterns.

  • A screen freezes because sorting 50k items runs in body. Fix: compute in the view model, once.
  • Release builds crash where Debug did not, because of force unwraps on optional data that previews never exercised.
  • A keyboard covers a text field on small phones because content was not placed in a scroll container; use ScrollView plus .scrollDismissesKeyboard and the automatic keyboard safe area.
  • App Store review flags accessibility-unfriendly UI rarely, but enterprise clients fail apps on Dynamic Type clipping.

Real industry examples. Sentry and Firebase Crashlytics reports from SwiftUI apps commonly show AttributeGraph frames in stack traces when a cycle or state mutation during update occurs. Seeing "AttributeGraph: cycle detected" in the console means a view's dependency loops (for example a GeometryReader writing to state that changes its own size).

Everyday analogy. The compiler error is a strict teacher who marks the whole page wrong because of one ink blot; find the blot by commenting out halves.

Common interview traps.

  • Hunting the long error text; the real fault is often a typo several lines above or a wrong type in a modifier.
  • Suppressing the "modifying state during view update" warning instead of moving the mutation.
  • Believing AnyView fixes type errors without cost.
  • Android vs iOS: Gradle errors are usually clear; SwiftUI type-check failures often point at the wrong line.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• SwiftUI and Compose share UI = f(state); a SwiftUI view is a cheap value-type description with a body, not a live UI object.
  • Identity (structural plus explicit) controls lifetime and state; if branches and .id create and destroy subtrees.
  • Modifiers wrap views inside out; order changes padding, background, frame and hit areas. This is inverted compared to how Compose is usually read.
  • Layout is propose, choose, place. .frame wraps and proposes; it does not resize.
  • Stacks hug content; Spacer and .frame(maxWidth: .infinity) fill. GeometryReader is greedy and should be used sparingly; prefer containerRelativeFrame and onGeometryChange (verify availability).
  • Layout, ViewThatFits and Grid (iOS 16+) cover custom and adaptive layouts; branch on size class, not device idiom.
  • @ViewBuilder powers content closures; prefer parameterised modifiers over conditionals that destroy identity.
  • Use #Preview with sample data; legacy PreviewProvider remains in old code.
  • Know the common compiler and runtime errors and the debugging tools: View Debugger, SwiftUI Instruments, _printChanges.
